newsitem.title: KENYA: Lufthansa may cancel ex-Kenya cargo flight.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa may cancel ex-Kenya cargo flight.

text.p: Lufthansa Cargo expects to cancel a Boeing 747 freighter from Nairobi later this week amid "serious concerns" over safety as air traffic controllers in Kenya entered their fifth day of a go-slow on Wednesday.
David Keary, general manager for East and Central Africa for Lufthansa Cargo, said he estimated total losses from the cargo load scheduled for Friday to be worth in the region of $400,000.
Keary said the go-slow combined with calls by Kenya's opposition for a general strike on Friday were factors which created a feeling of insecurity in the industry.

"We are strongly considering cancelling the Friday flight, I am worried about the safety already, but if the general strike takes off, usually the first thing which will be hit is the transport sector.

"The fire brigade, the meteorological department. All the essential requirements needed to handle an operation appears to be in jeopardy. Even the staff needed to handle the aircraft might not be there and we could be faced with a situation where nobody would be there when we come in," Keary told Reuters.

He said Friday's cargo shipment of between 60 and 70 tonnes consisted of cut flowers, vegetables and fresh fish for European markets and unless urgent improvements would take place at the Nairobi airport Lufthansa would be forced to cancel the flight.

Keary also said European importers were now starting to look at alternative producer countries for flower and other fresh produce imports due to the delays since the go-slow was started last Friday midnight.
"I've just talked to importers in Europe, including one major importer who takes 20 tonnes a day, and they are already looking for other flowers from outside Kenya.
"He will come back once things get back to normal, but as long as the unrest stays in place it's a quite considerable load which is lost," said Keary.

He said he had spent all of Tuesday to "try minimise damage and co-ordinate things", but the industry was getting "worried and concerned" about the losses and damages caused by the continuing go-slow at Nairobi.

Business has been crippled and both tourists and air cargo have been facing major delays of up to 12 hours or more since the air traffic controllers went on strike demanding better pay and working conditions.
Kenya produced more than 90,000 tonnes of flowers, fruits and vegetables in 1996 of which more than 90 percent was exported by air.

"Twenty-four hours is the maximum for perishable products to be delayed, just a few hours mean the goods will miss the marketing date in Europe, they will lose the distribution connection, the products are not as fresh as they could be and they will start to lose value," said Keary.
Air traffic controllers in all Kenyan airports on Wednesday ignored a government order to resume work and said they would continue the go-slow until their demands were met.

Separately in London, Kenya Airways said in a statement thatthe extent of the delays varies on a daily basis and "inbound delays are averaging two to three hours and problems with incoming persihables have been minimal". - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
